title: The Ottoman Hejaz
subtitle: 1517–1900 · The Guardianship of the Ḥaramayn, the Wahhābī Interlude, the Steamship Hajj and the Northwest Oases

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Four centuries of Ottoman guardianship over a tax-exempt sacred province, broken once by the Wahhābī–Saudi occupation and the Egyptian reconquest, then reasserted as a directly ruled vilayet — with the northwest oases a tribal borderland the pilgrim road crossed

entries.group: The Ottoman Guardianship and the Sharifate (1517–1803)
entries.label: The Ottoman guardianship begins
entries.hint: After Selim I took Egypt, the sharif Barakāt II sent his son to submit. The Ottomans confirmed the sharif in office, assumed the guardianship of the two holy cities, and took over the kiswa, the grain and the organisation of the pilgrim caravans.
entries.note: al-Nahrawālī, al-Iʿlām bi-aʿlām bayt Allāh al-ḥarām; Suraiya Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans: The Hajj under the Ottomans' (1994).

entries.group: The Ottoman Guardianship and the Sharifate (1517–1803)
entries.label: The sharifs of Mecca under the Ottomans
entries.hint: The Qatādid dynasty continued, its Dhawū Zayd and Dhawū Barakāt branches feuding for the emirate, with Istanbul confirming, deposing and occasionally sending troops to impose a sharif of its choice.
entries.note: Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); the Ottoman records of sharifian appointments.

entries.group: The Ottoman Guardianship and the Sharifate (1517–1803)
entries.label: The Sürre and the privileged province
entries.hint: The Hejaz paid no tax. Instead Istanbul sent the annual Sürre — a caravan of money and grain for the mosques, the sharif, the scholars and the poor — and organised and subsidised the Damascus and Egyptian Hajj caravans. The province was governed as a trust.
entries.note: the Sürre registers in the Ottoman archives; Faroqhi (1994).

entries.group: The Wahhābī Interlude and the Egyptian Reconquest (1803–1840)
entries.label: The First Saudi State takes the Hejaz
entries.loc: Mecca, Medina and Ṭāʾif, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The Wahhābī–Saudi forces took Ṭāʾif, Mecca and Medina, expelled the Ottoman-backed sharif, stopped the imperial Hajj, demolished the domed tombs of the Baqīʿ, and imposed the doctrine — the gravest challenge to the Ottoman guardianship in three centuries.
entries.note: Burckhardt, 'Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys' (1830); the Saudi chronicles.

entries.group: The Wahhābī Interlude and the Egyptian Reconquest (1803–1840)
entries.label: The Egyptian reconquest and administration
entries.hint: On the sultan's order, Egyptian armies under Ṭūsūn and Ibrāhīm Pasha retook the Hejaz from the Saudis. Egypt then administered the province, restored the sharifate and the sanctuary practice, and held it until the 1840 settlement forced its withdrawal.
entries.note: Burckhardt, 'Travels in Arabia' (1829); the Egyptian sources on the Hejaz administration.

entries.group: The Restored Ottoman Hejaz and the Vilayet (1840–1900)
entries.label: Direct rule and the Vilayet of the Hejaz
entries.hint: After Egypt left, the Ottomans reasserted direct control, created the Vilayet of the Hejaz in 1872 under a governor at Jeddah, and kept the sharif as a subordinate — a tighter grip driven by the Wahhābī scare and by the province's new value for the pan-Islamic policy of Abdülhamid II.
entries.note: William Ochsenwald, 'Religion, Society, and the State in Arabia: The Hijaz under Ottoman Control, 1840–1908' (1984).

entries.group: The Northwest: the Oases and the Pilgrim Road (1517–1900)
entries.label: The oases of the northwest
entries.loc: al-ʿUlā, Taymāʾ, Khaybar and Tabūk, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The northern oases — al-ʿUlā, Taymāʾ, Khaybar, Tabūk, Dūmat al-Jandal — lay under nominal Ottoman and sharifian authority but real tribal control: the ʿAnaza, the Balī, the Ḥuwayṭāt and the Rwala. The Syrian Hajj caravan was the one institution that reached them.
entries.note: C. M. Doughty, 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888); Alois Musil's later surveys of the northern Hejaz.

entries.group: The Northwest: the Oases and the Pilgrim Road (1517–1900)
entries.label: The Hajj-road forts and the amīr al-ḥajj
entries.loc: Tabūk, al-Muʿaẓẓam and al-Ḥijr, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The Ottomans built and garrisoned a chain of forts along the Syrian pilgrim route — Tabūk, al-Muʿaẓẓam, al-ʿUlā, al-Ḥijr — each with a cistern, and paid the tribes a subsidy to let the caravan pass. The amīr al-ḥajj who led it from Damascus was a great Ottoman office.
entries.note: Andrew Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan' (2012); the Ottoman fort inscriptions.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The sharifian civil wars, the Wahhābī occupation and the Egyptian campaigns to end it, the collision with Europe at Jeddah in 1858, and the chronic war of the tribes and the caravan

entries.label: The sharifian civil wars
entries.hint: The Dhawū Zayd–Dhawū Barakāt feud and the wider quarrels of the Meccan sharifs, fought out over three centuries with Ottoman troops, Egyptian arbitration and tribal levies — the normal politics of the emirate.
entries.note: Faroqhi (1994); the Ottoman military interventions recorded in the Hejaz chronicles.

entries.label: The Saudi conquest of the Hejaz
entries.loc: Ṭāʾif, Mecca and Medina, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The massacre at Ṭāʾif in 1802, the taking of Mecca and Medina, the demolition of the shrines and the closing of the Ottoman Hajj — the Wahhābī interlude as an armed occupation of the holiest ground in Islam.
entries.note: Burckhardt, 'Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys' (1830); the Saudi chronicles.

entries.label: The Egyptian campaigns
entries.hint: Ṭūsūn's and Ibrāhīm Pasha's wars to retake the Hejaz and then to pursue the Saudis into Najd, fought with Egyptian artillery and levies against forces that had no answer to cannon.
entries.note: Burckhardt (1829); the Egyptian campaign records.

entries.label: The Jeddah massacre
entries.hint: A mob killed the British and French consuls and a number of Christian and local residents. A British warship bombarded the town and the Ottomans executed the ringleaders — an early, violent collision of the closed Hejaz with European power.
entries.note: the British and French consular reports; Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020).

entries.label: The Bedouin and the Hajj
entries.loc: the Syrian and Egyptian pilgrim routes
entries.hint: The raiding of the pilgrim caravans by the tribes of the route, the surra payments that bought passage, and the periodic disasters when a subsidy lapsed or a caravan was caught — a low, chronic war along the whole road, and a constant Ottoman expense.
entries.note: Faroqhi (1994); the Ottoman correspondence on the tribal subsidies; the accounts of caravan attacks in the traveller literature.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A sacred province governed with a deliberately light hand, the state logistics of the Hajj, the endowment system that funded it, the Egyptian interlude's reforms, and the international quarantine regime

entries.label: The administration of a sacred province
entries.hint: The qāḍī of Mecca, a top post in the imperial religious hierarchy appointed from Istanbul for a year, the governor at Jeddah, the tax exemption, and a deliberate light touch — the Hejaz was administered as a trust to be protected, not a territory to be exploited.
entries.note: Ochsenwald, 'Religion, Society, and the State in Arabia' (1984); Faroqhi (1994).

entries.label: The organisation of the Hajj
entries.loc: Damascus and Cairo · to the Ḥaramayn
entries.hint: The amīr al-ḥajj of Damascus and of Cairo, the fixed stages and forts, the subsidy to the tribes, the kiswa and the maḥmal — a logistical operation moving tens of thousands of people across the desert on a schedule, run by the Ottoman state.
entries.note: Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); Jomier on the Egyptian maḥmal.

entries.label: The waqf al-Ḥaramayn and the Sürre
entries.loc: across the empire · for the two holy cities
entries.hint: Endowments across the empire dedicated to the two mosques, administered from Istanbul, plus the annual imperial gift of money and grain — the financial system that kept the Hejaz solvent, fed and loyal without taxing it.
entries.note: the awqāf al-Ḥaramayn administration; Miriam Hoexter and Faroqhi on the endowment system.

entries.label: The Egyptian interlude's reforms
entries.hint: Muḥammad ʿAlī's administration introduced a regular garrison, reorganised the Jeddah customs, and dealt more firmly with the sharifs and the tribes — a preview of the direct Ottoman rule that followed after 1840.
entries.note: Ochsenwald (1984); the Egyptian administrative records.

entries.label: Quarantine and the international regulation of the Hajj
entries.hint: After the 1865 cholera pandemic the international sanitary conferences imposed quarantine stations, medical inspection of pilgrim ships and limits on numbers — the first international regulation of a religious rite, and a European hand laid on the Ottoman Hejaz.
entries.note: Valeska Huber, 'The Unification of the Globe by Disease? The International Sanitary Conferences on Cholera, 1851–1894'; the Kamaran quarantine records.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Sunni establishment restored after the Wahhābī interlude, the Ḥaramayn as a crossroads of Islamic reform, the huge resident scholarly communities, and the Hejaz at the centre of Abdülhamid's pan-Islam

entries.label: The Sunni establishment restored
entries.hint: After the Wahhābī interlude the Ottomans reinstated the four schools, the shrine visitation, the mawlid and the Sufi orders, and made the suppression of 'Wahhābism' a standing concern of the Mecca qāḍī and the governor.
entries.note: Ochsenwald (1984); the Ottoman anti-Wahhābī fatwās and administrative circulars.

entries.label: The Ḥaramayn as a hub of Islamic reform
entries.hint: Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Mecca and Medina were where the founders of the great modern Sufi and reform movements met and studied — Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, the founders of the Sanūsiyya and the Khatmiyya, the Naqshbandī-Mujaddidī — a crossroads of ideas that spread from West Africa to Indonesia.
entries.note: John Voll, 'Islam: Continuity and Change in the Modern World' (1982); R. S. O'Fahey, 'Enigmatic Saint: Ahmad ibn Idris' (1990).

entries.label: The Jāwa colony and the global ʿulamāʾ
entries.hint: The resident scholarly communities of Mecca — the 'Jāwa' from the Malay world, the Indians, the Central Asians, the West Africans — grew huge in the 19th century, and the Meccan teachers of the Jāwa, above all Nawawī al-Bantanī, shaped the Islam of Southeast Asia.
entries.note: C. Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89), on the Jāwa colony; Michael Laffan, 'Islamic Nationhood and Colonial Indonesia' (2003).

entries.label: Pan-Islam and the Hejaz under Abdülhamid II
entries.hint: The sultan-caliph made the guardianship of the two holy cities and the welfare of the pilgrims the centrepiece of a pan-Islamic policy — the Sürre, the coming railway, the emphasis on the caliphal title — aimed at the Muslims of the British, French, Dutch and Russian empires.
entries.note: Selim Deringil, 'The Well-Protected Domains' (1998); Kemal Karpat, 'The Politicization of Islam' (2001).

entries.label: The Shiʿi and the vanished Jews of the north
entries.loc: Medina and the northern oases, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The Nakhāwila Shiʿa of Medina, the Shiʿi and Zaydī pilgrims and residents, and — a memory by this period rather than a reality — the Jewish communities of Khaybar and the northern oases, long since gone, though 19th-century travellers still asked after them.
entries.note: Werner Ende on the Nakhāwila; the traveller accounts (Doughty, Wallin) chasing the legend of the Jews of Khaybar.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Ottoman Kaʿba and the domed colonnades of the Ḥaramayn, the coral houses of old Jeddah, the pilgrim-road forts, the mass-produced pilgrim image, and the limited public music of the season

entries.label: The Ottoman Kaʿba and the Ḥaramayn
entries.hint: Murad IV's rebuilding of the Kaʿba after the flood of 1630 gave it the form it keeps today, and the Ottomans added domed colonnades, minarets and mosaics to the two mosques over four centuries — the last great imperial phase of building at the Ḥaramayn.
entries.note: the Ottoman rebuilding accounts; the pre-modern photographs and plans of the Ḥaramayn.

entries.label: Old Jeddah (al-Balad)
entries.hint: The tall coral-stone merchant houses with their carved wooden rawāshīn balconies, built on the Hajj and the Red Sea trade, gave old Jeddah a distinctive Red Sea urban form — now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
entries.note: Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020); the al-Balad UNESCO nomination file (2014).

entries.label: The forts of the Hajj road
entries.loc: Tabūk, al-Muʿaẓẓam and Dhāt Ḥajj, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The squat Ottoman qalʿas along the Syrian and Egyptian pilgrim routes — each a fortified cistern and store — are the visible infrastructure of the imperial Hajj across the northwest desert, and among the best-preserved Ottoman military architecture in Arabia.
entries.note: Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan' (2012); the Saudi surveys of the Darb al-Ḥajj al-Shāmī.

entries.label: The pilgrim image, from the prayer book to the photograph
entries.loc: Mecca · and across the Muslim world
entries.hint: The enormously popular prayer book Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt, with its schematic paintings of the two mosques, was carried by pilgrims everywhere — and from the 1880s Snouck Hurgronje's photographs, taken with a Meccan assistant, became the first images of the holy city.
entries.note: the Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt manuscript tradition; Snouck Hurgronje's 'Bilder-Atlas zu Mekka' (1889).

entries.label: The music of the season
entries.loc: Mecca, Ṭāʾif and the caravan route
entries.hint: The drums and shawms of the maḥmal procession, the sharifs' court musicians at Ṭāʾif, and the work-songs of the water-carriers and the pilgrim guides — a limited public music in a city where the strict religious currents disapproved of it.
entries.note: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89), on Meccan music and the guilds; Lisa Urkevich, 'Music and Traditions of the Arabian Peninsula' (2015).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Europeans who did the Hajj in disguise and published, the opening of the northwest to Western scholarship, Snouck Hurgronje's Mekka, and the new science of the pilgrimage's diseases

entries.label: Burckhardt and Burton
entries.loc: Mecca and Medina · described in disguise
entries.hint: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt's 'Travels in Arabia' (1829), the first accurate European account of the holy cities by a man who did the Hajj, and Richard Burton's 'Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to Al-Madinah and Meccah' (1855) — the founding texts of the Western literature on the Hejaz.
entries.note: J. L. Burckhardt, 'Travels in Arabia' (1829); Richard F. Burton, 'Personal Narrative' (1855–56).

entries.label: Doughty, Euting and the northwest
entries.loc: Taymāʾ, Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ and al-ʿUlā, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Charles Doughty's 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888), mostly about the northern oases, and the 1883–84 journey of Charles Huber and Julius Euting that recovered the Aramaic Taymāʾ Stone — the northwest opened to Western scholarship, at the cost of Huber's murder near the coast in 1884.
entries.note: C. M. Doughty, 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888); Julius Euting, 'Tagbuch einer Reise in Inner-Arabien' (1896); the Taymāʾ Stone, now in the Louvre.

entries.label: Snouck Hurgronje's Mekka
entries.hint: The Dutch orientalist lived in Mecca in 1884–85 and wrote 'Mekka', a detailed ethnography of the city, its scholars, its guilds and its Jāwa colony — the classic account of the late-Ottoman Hejaz, and, in service of Dutch colonial policy in the Indies, a work of intelligence.
entries.note: C. Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Michael Laffan and others on its colonial context.

entries.label: The medicine of the Hajj
entries.loc: Mecca · reported to the sanitary conferences
entries.hint: The epidemiological literature that grew from the 19th-century cholera pandemics — the Ottoman and Egyptian sanitary services, the reports to the international conferences, the debate over whether to restrict the pilgrimage — made the Hajj a subject of modern public health.
entries.note: Adrien Proust, 'Essai sur l'hygiène internationale' (1873); the proceedings of the International Sanitary Conferences (1866, 1874, 1885, 1894).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A city that produced nothing and lived on the pilgrimage, Jeddah as the Red Sea port, the steamship mass-Hajj, and a slave trade that ran through the holiest ground in Islam

entries.label: The Hajj as the whole economy
entries.hint: Pilgrim spending, the hereditary Meccan guilds of guides, camel-brokers and water-carriers, the Jeddah customs, and the imperial subsidies — Mecca produced almost nothing and lived entirely on the pilgrimage and the piety of the empire.
entries.note: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Ochsenwald (1984).

entries.label: Jeddah, the Red Sea port
entries.hint: The harbour handled the sea pilgrims and a transit trade in coffee, spices, pearls and grain between the Indian Ocean, Egypt and the Levant. Its merchant houses — Indian, Hadrami, local — were the Hejaz's real capitalists.
entries.note: Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah: The Gate to Mecca in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries' (2020).

entries.label: The steamship Hajj
entries.hint: From the 1850s and especially after the Suez Canal in 1869, steamships carried pilgrims to Jeddah in tens of thousands from India, the Dutch East Indies and the Ottoman ports — a mass pilgrimage that transformed the scale, the economics and the danger of the Hajj.
entries.note: John Slight, 'The British Empire and the Hajj, 1865–1956' (2015); Eric Tagliacozzo, 'The Longest Journey' (2013).

entries.label: The slave trade through Jeddah
entries.hint: Enslaved Africans from Sudan and Ethiopia, shipped via Suakin and Massawa, were sold at Jeddah and Mecca, some to pilgrims, some manumitted at the holy sites. British and half-hearted Ottoman measures from the 1850s reduced but did not end the traffic before 1900.
entries.note: Ehud Toledano, 'The Ottoman Slave Trade and Its Suppression' (1982); William Gervase Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The forts and cisterns that made the pilgrim road passable, the steamship-telegraph-quarantine grid, and the railway begun in 1900

entries.label: The forts and cisterns of the pilgrim road
entries.loc: the Syrian route, Tabūk to Medina
entries.hint: The Ottoman qalʿas and their stone reservoirs along the Syrian route were the water and security infrastructure without which the caravan could not have crossed the northwest desert — the one thing the empire built and maintained in the region.
entries.note: Petersen (2012); the Saudi and Jordanian surveys of the Ottoman Hajj forts.

entries.label: Steam, telegraph and quarantine
entries.hint: The steamship that remade the Hajj, the telegraph line that reached Jeddah and Mecca in the 1880s, and the quarantine stations and disinfection plants at Kamaran and al-Ṭūr — the Hejaz wired into the imperial and international grid.
entries.note: Deringil, 'The Well-Protected Domains' (1998); Valeska Huber on the sanitary infrastructure.

entries.label: The Hejaz Railway begins
entries.hint: Abdülhamid II authorised in 1900 a railway from Damascus to Medina, funded by donations from Muslims worldwide and built by the Ottoman army — a project of pilgrimage, strategy and pan-Islamic prestige, begun at the very end of this folio.
entries.note: William Ochsenwald, 'The Hijaz Railroad' (1980); the railway's completion to Medina in 1908 belongs to the next folio.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The guardianship as the empire's most valuable intangible asset, the Hajj as the umma's assembly and an anti-colonial listening post, the arrival of Europe, and the northwest as a claimed and ungoverned borderland

entries.label: Istanbul and the guardianship
entries.hint: The Ottoman sultan-caliph's guardianship of the two holy cities was the empire's most valuable non-material asset — the basis of the caliphal claim, the argument for its leadership of the Sunni world, and, under Abdülhamid, a lever against the European powers.
entries.note: Deringil (1998); Karpat, 'The Politicization of Islam' (2001).

entries.label: The Hajj as the umma's assembly
entries.hint: The pilgrimage kept its role as the great annual meeting — of scholars, books, goods and disease, and increasingly in the 19th century of anti-colonial politics, which the British, Dutch and French watched closely through their Jeddah consulates.
entries.note: Slight, 'The British Empire and the Hajj' (2015); Tagliacozzo, 'The Longest Journey' (2013).

entries.label: Europe reaches the Hejaz
entries.hint: The Jeddah consulates, the sanitary regime, the naval bombardment of 1858 and the disguised travellers — the beginning of a European presence in and pressure on a region that had been closed to non-Muslims for a thousand years.
entries.note: Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020); the consular archives.

entries.label: The Meccan networks of the colonised Muslim world
entries.loc: Mecca · to the Indies, India and Africa
entries.hint: The Jāwa, Indian and West African communities at Mecca were channels back to the Dutch East Indies, British India and French Africa, carrying reformist and, later, anti-colonial ideas home with the returning pilgrims — a flow the colonial powers tried and failed to monitor.
entries.note: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Laffan, 'Islamic Nationhood and Colonial Indonesia' (2003).

entries.label: The northwest as tribal borderland
entries.loc: al-Jawf, Taymāʾ and Tabūk, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The oases and routes of the northwest lay between the Ottoman Hejaz, the sharifate, the Rashīdī and Saudi Najd, and the confederations of the Syrian desert — claimed by all and governed by none, crossed twice a year by the pilgrimage.
entries.note: Doughty (1888); the later British and Ottoman surveys of the northern Hejaz frontier.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The empire's most sacred and least profitable province, the Wahhābī interlude as a permanent warning, and the steamship's transformation of the Hajj into a global mass event and a disease vector

entries.label: The most sacred and least profitable province
entries.hint: The Ottomans held the Hejaz at a permanent loss, for the legitimacy the guardianship conferred. It paid no tax, cost the Sürre and the caravan subsidies, and its politics were managed by payment rather than by force.
entries.note: Ochsenwald (1984); Faroqhi (1994).

entries.label: The Wahhābī interlude as a lasting lesson
entries.hint: The 1803–1818 Saudi occupation of the Ḥaramayn showed how fragile the guardianship was, and made the containment of the Wahhābī–Saudi movement a fixed priority — Ottoman, then Egyptian, then British — for a century.
entries.note: Ochsenwald (1984); the recurring Ottoman anxiety about a second Saudi advance.

entries.label: Steam remakes the Hajj
entries.hint: Within a generation the pilgrimage went from a caravan of thousands to a shipborne mass of hundreds of thousands — bigger, cheaper, more global, and a recurring vector of cholera (some fifteen thousand dead at Mecca in 1865) that made the Hejaz an object of international regulation.
entries.note: Valeska Huber on the sanitary conferences; the WHO retrospectives on Hajj cholera. Casualty figures are contemporary estimates.

entries.label: The thread continues — the railway, the Sharif Hussein and the Revolt
entries.hint: The folio ends in 1900 with the Hejaz Railway authorised and the Vilayet in place. The railway's completion to Medina in 1908, Sharif Hussein's appointment, the Arab Revolt of 1916 and the short-lived Hashemite kingdom are the next folio.
entries.note: a forward reference: hejaz-1900-1925 (the railway, the Arab Revolt and the Kingdom of the Hejaz) is planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The guilds of Mecca, the resident foreign communities, the slave market amid the holy sites, and the women of the mass pilgrimage

entries.label: The mutawwifūn and the guilds
entries.hint: The hereditary guild of pilgrim guides, each family licensed to serve pilgrims from a particular country, and the guilds of camel-brokers, water-carriers and porters — a whole urban economy and society organised around receiving the Hajj.
entries.note: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89), on the guild system; later studies of the mutawwif institution.

entries.label: The Jāwa, Indian and African communities
entries.hint: The resident foreigners of Mecca — students, merchants, freed slaves, exiles — many of whom never left, formed settled communities that Snouck Hurgronje mapped and that made Mecca one of the most cosmopolitan cities on earth.
entries.note: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Tagliacozzo and Toorawa (eds), 'The Hajj: Pilgrimage in Islam' (2016).

entries.label: The slave market and manumission
entries.hint: The Jeddah and Mecca slave markets, the enslaved Africans who arrived with the pilgrim traffic, and the custom of freeing a slave at the holy sites — the same ground where slavery was practised was where, ritually, it was undone.
entries.note: Toledano, 'The Ottoman Slave Trade' (1982); Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006).

entries.label: Women on the Hajj
entries.hint: Women came in growing numbers, especially by steamship, under the maḥram rules; the sanitary regime's inspection of women pilgrims caused particular scandal; and the few surviving accounts by women pilgrims are a rare window on the experience of the Hajj.
entries.note: the accounts of women pilgrims (e.g. Lady Evelyn Cobbold, later; the earlier Ottoman women's Hajj memoirs); Marjo Buitelaar on women and the Hajj.
